nodes.description: A game engine is a software framework that provides the core systems needed to build and run games, including rendering, physics, audio, input handling, scripting, and asset management. Engines abstract away low-level platform details so developers can focus on gameplay logic and content. Examples include Unity, Unreal Engine, Godot, and custom in-house solutions.

resources.title: Choosing a Game Engine is Easy!

nodes.name: Unity 3D
nodes.description: **Unity 3D** is a versatile, cross-platform game engine that supports the development of both 2D and 3D games. This game engine allows users to create a wide variety of games including AR, VR, Mobile, Consoles, and Computers in C#. It provides a host of powerful features and tools, such as scripting, asset bundling, scene building, and simulation, to assist developers in creating interactive content. Unity 3D also boasts a large, active community that regularly contributes tutorials, scripts, assets, and more, making it a robust platform for all levels of game developers.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine
nodes.description: The **Unreal Engine** is a powerful game development engine created by Epic Games. Used by game developers worldwide, it supports the creation of high-quality games across multiple platforms such as iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, Xbox, and PlayStation. Unreal Engine is renowned for its photo-realistic rendering, dynamic physics and effects, robust multiplayer framework, and its flexible scripting system called Blueprint. The engine is also fully equipped with dedicated tools and functionalities for animation, AI, lighting, cinematography, and post-processing effects. The most recent version, Unreal Engine 5, introduces real-time Global Illumination and makes film-quality real-time graphics achievable.

nodes.name: Native
nodes.description: You don't necessarily have to use tools like Unreal, Unity3d, or Godot to make games. You can also use native languages like C++ or Rust to make games. However, you will have to do a lot of work yourself, and you will have to learn a lot of things that are already done for you in game engines.

nodes.name: Godot
nodes.description: Godot is an open-source, multi-platform game engine that is known for being feature-rich and user-friendly. It is developed by hundreds of contributors from around the world and supports the creation of both 2D and 3D games. Godot uses its own scripting language, GDScript, which is similar to Python, but it also supports C#. It is equipped with a unique scene system and comes with a multitude of tools that can expedite the development process. Godot's design philosophy centers around flexibility, extensibility, and ease of use, providing a handy tool for both beginners and pros in game development.

resources.title: Tutorial - How to make a Video Game in Godot
Tutorial - How to make 3D Games in Godot

nodes.name: Game Physics
nodes.description: Game physics simulates physical behavior in a game world, including rigid body dynamics, collision detection, constraints, and fluid or soft body effects. Physics engines abstract the mathematics of Newtonian mechanics into systems that update object positions and velocities each frame. Popular physics middleware includes Bullet, PhysX, Havok, and Box2D.

nodes.name: Collision Detection
nodes.description: Collision detection is the process of determining when and where two objects in a simulation intersect or make contact. It is divided into broad phase, which quickly eliminates non-colliding pairs, and narrow phase, which computes exact contact geometry. The output of collision detection feeds into the collision response system to resolve penetrations and apply impulses.

nodes.name: CCD
nodes.description: Continuous Collision Detection (CCD) prevents fast-moving objects from tunneling through thin geometry by testing for collisions along the entire swept path of an object between frames, rather than just at the start and end positions. Without CCD, a bullet or fast projectile can pass entirely through a wall in a single time step. CCD is more expensive than discrete detection and is typically enabled selectively for fast-moving objects.

nodes.name: Narrow Phase
nodes.description: Narrow phase collision detection performs precise geometric intersection tests between pairs of objects that the broad phase has flagged as potential collisions. It computes contact points, contact normals, and penetration depths needed for the physics solver. Algorithms used in narrow phase include GJK, EPA, and SAT, depending on the shape types involved.

nodes.name: Intersection
nodes.description: Intersection tests determine whether two geometric shapes overlap in space. These tests are used throughout physics and rendering to answer questions like whether a ray hit a surface or whether two colliders are touching. Different shape pairs (sphere-sphere, box-triangle, capsule-mesh) require different algorithms with varying cost and precision tradeoffs.

nodes.name: SAT
nodes.description: The Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) is a method for detecting collisions between convex shapes. It works by testing a set of axes and checking whether the projections of two shapes onto each axis overlap. If any axis produces a gap, the shapes are not colliding; if all axes show overlap, a collision is confirmed.

resources.title: Collision Detection Using the Separating Axis Theorem

nodes.name: GJK
nodes.description: The **GJK algorithm** (Gilbert–Johnson–Keerthi) is a computational geometry algorithm that is widely used to detect collisions between convex objects in video games and simulations. The primary role of this algorithm is to assess the intersection between two convex shapes. What makes it unique and widely used is its efficiency and accuracy even when dealing with complex three-dimensional shapes. It uses the concept of "Minkowski Difference" to simplify its calculations and determine if two shapes are intersecting.

nodes.name: EPA
nodes.description: The **EPA** (Expanding Polytope Algorithm) is an iterative algorithm used for calculating the penetration depth between two shapes in collision detection. It is commonly used in physics engines and robotics. The algorithm takes the resulting simplex from a previously applied GJK algorithm, iteratively expanding the polytope towards the Minkowski Difference boundary until it finds the closest point to the origin. The vector from that point to the origin is the penetration vector and its magnitude is equal to the penetration depth between the two shapes.

resources.title: EPA: Collision response algorithm for 2D/3D - winter.dev

nodes.name: Convexity
nodes.description: Convexity describes the property of a shape where any line segment connecting two points inside the shape remains entirely inside it. Convex shapes are simpler to process in physics simulations because algorithms like GJK can solve intersection and distance queries efficiently for them. Non-convex meshes are usually decomposed into convex parts for simulation.

nodes.name: Convex
nodes.description: The term "convex" in game development relates primarily to shapes and collision detection within the gaming environment. A shape is convex if all line segments between any two points in the shape lie entirely within the shape. This is an essential concept when programming collision detection and physics engines in games since the mathematical calculations can be more straightforward and efficient when the objects are convex. In addition to this, many rendering algorithms also operate optimally on convex objects, thereby helping improve the game’s graphical performance.

nodes.name: Convex Hull
nodes.description: A convex hull is the smallest convex shape that fully contains a set of points. In game development, convex hulls are generated from mesh vertices to produce physics colliders that approximate the original shape while remaining usable by convex-only physics algorithms. Most physics engines provide tools to compute convex hulls from arbitrary geometry automatically.

nodes.name: Broad Phase
nodes.description: **Broad Phase Collision Detection** is the first step in the collision detection process. Its primary function is to identify which pairs of objects might potentially collide. Rather than examining the entire body of every object for possible collision, it wraps up each one in a simpler shape like a bounding box or sphere, aiming to reduce the number of calculations. The output of this phase is a list of 'candidate pairs' which are passed onto the next phase, often referred to as the narrow phase, for in-depth overlap checks.

nodes.name: Bounding Volume
nodes.description: `Bounding Volume` is a simple shape that fully encompasses a more complex game model. It is less expensive to check for the intersection of bounding volumes when compared to checking for intersection of the actual models. Some commonly used types of bounding volume in game development include Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs), Bounding Spheres, and Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs). AABBs and Bounding Spheres are simple to implement and work well with static objects, while OBBs are slightly more complex and are often used with dynamic objects that need to rotate.

nodes.name: AABB
nodes.description: An AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) is a rectangular bounding volume whose edges are always aligned with the world coordinate axes. It is one of the simplest and fastest bounding volume types to compute and test for overlap. Because it does not rotate with the object, it must be recalculated whenever the object moves or rotates, which makes it most efficient for static or slowly moving objects.

nodes.name: Concave
nodes.description: A concave shape has at least one surface that curves inward, meaning a line segment between two interior points may pass outside the boundary. Concave meshes cannot be used directly in many physics algorithms without decomposition. In games, concave shapes are often reserved for static terrain or environments, with dynamic objects approximated using convex hulls or compound colliders.

nodes.name: Convex Decomposition
nodes.description: Convex decomposition breaks a concave mesh into a set of convex pieces that together approximate the original shape. This allows concave objects to be simulated in physics engines that require convex geometry by treating the decomposed parts as a compound collider. Algorithms like V-HACD are commonly used to automate this process.

nodes.name: Spatial Partitioning
nodes.description: Spatial partitioning divides a scene into regions to accelerate queries like collision detection, ray casting, and visibility culling. By organizing objects into a structure that reflects their position in space, the engine can quickly discard large portions of the scene that are irrelevant to a given query. Common data structures include grids, octrees, BSP trees, and BVHs.

nodes.name: Sort & Sweep
nodes.description: Sort and sweep, also called sweep and prune, is a broad-phase collision detection technique. Objects' bounding volumes are projected onto one or more axes, and the projections are sorted. Pairs whose projections overlap on all axes are flagged as potential collision candidates for narrow-phase testing.

nodes.name: BVH
nodes.description: A BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy) is a tree structure where leaf nodes contain individual objects and each internal node contains a bounding volume that encloses all its children. BVHs are widely used for ray tracing and broad-phase collision detection. Traversal is fast because entire subtrees can be discarded when the query does not intersect a node's bounding volume.

nodes.name: DBVT
nodes.description: A DBVT (Dynamic Bounding Volume Tree) is a variant of BVH designed for scenes where objects move frequently. Rather than rebuilding the entire tree on each frame, a DBVT supports incremental updates by reinserting or refitting only the affected nodes. The Bullet physics engine popularized this approach for real-time dynamic collision broadphase.

nodes.name: Stencil Shadow
nodes.description: Stencil shadows, also called shadow volumes, are a technique where the shadow boundary of an object is extruded into a volume and used to mark shadowed pixels in the stencil buffer. For each fragment, the algorithm counts how many shadow volumes surround it to determine whether it is in shadow. This method produces sharp, accurate shadows but is expensive for complex geometry.

resources.title: The Mechanics of Robust Stencil Shadows

nodes.name: Programming Languages
nodes.description: Programming languages are the tools used to implement game logic, engine systems, and tooling. Different languages suit different parts of game development: C++ for performance-critical engine code, C# for scripting in Unity, Python for tools, and Rust for systems programming. Language choice affects performance, iteration speed, and the size of the available ecosystem.

nodes.name: C#
nodes.description: C# is a statically typed, object-oriented language developed by Microsoft and used as the primary scripting language in Unity. It runs on the .NET runtime and features garbage collection, LINQ, and strong tooling support. C# offers a balance between developer productivity and runtime performance suitable for game logic.

nodes.name: C/C++
nodes.description: C and C++ are the dominant languages for game engine development and performance-critical game code. C++ offers object-oriented features, templates, and direct memory management, making it suitable for building engines, physics systems, and rendering pipelines. Most major game engines are written in C++ or expose C++ APIs for custom extensions.

nodes.name: Rust
nodes.description: Rust is a systems programming language focused on memory safety and performance without a garbage collector. In game development, Rust is used for engine components, tools, and increasingly for full game projects through frameworks like Bevy. Its ownership model eliminates whole classes of bugs common in C++ codebases.

nodes.name: Python
nodes.description: Python is a high-level, dynamically typed language used in game development primarily for tooling, automation, and scripting. Its readable syntax and large standard library make it practical for build pipelines, content generation, and prototype logic. Godot supports Python-like GDScript, and some engines offer Python scripting bindings.

nodes.name: GDScript
nodes.description: GDScript is the primary scripting language for the Godot game engine, designed to be easy to learn and tightly integrated with the engine's node system. Its syntax resembles Python, making it accessible to beginners while remaining capable enough for production games. GDScript is interpreted at runtime and can interact directly with Godot's built-in types and classes.

resources.title: How to program in Godot - GDScript Tutorial

nodes.name: OBB
nodes.description: An OBB (Oriented Bounding Box) is a rectangular bounding volume that can rotate freely to match the orientation of the object it encloses. Compared to an AABB, an OBB typically provides a tighter fit, reducing false positives in collision tests. Intersection tests between OBBs are more expensive than AABB tests, usually implemented using SAT.

nodes.name: Computer Graphics
nodes.description: Computer graphics is the field concerned with generating and manipulating visual content using computers. In game development it covers rendering techniques, shading, geometry processing, and the mathematical foundations behind producing images from 3D scenes. Understanding computer graphics is required for working with rendering pipelines, shaders, and visual effects.

resources.title: How do Video Game Graphics Work?

nodes.name: Rendering Equation
nodes.description: The rendering equation, introduced by Kajiya in 1986, describes the total light leaving a surface point in a given direction as the sum of emitted light and incoming light reflected from all directions. It provides the theoretical basis for physically based rendering. Solving the rendering equation exactly is computationally intractable, so real-time and offline renderers use various approximations and importance sampling strategies.

nodes.name: Mapping
nodes.description: Mapping in graphics refers to techniques that apply 2D images or data to 3D surfaces to add detail without increasing geometry count. Texture mapping, normal mapping, parallax mapping, and horizon mapping are all variations that serve different purposes, from adding color and surface texture to simulating depth and complex lighting responses.

resources.title: Mapping and Tiles in Game Development

nodes.name: Texture
nodes.description: Textures are 2D images applied to 3D surfaces to provide color, detail, or surface data like roughness and normals. They are sampled by shaders during rendering using UV coordinates mapped onto geometry. Mip-mapping and texture compression are used to manage memory and performance at different viewing distances.

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.description: Reflection describes how light bounces off a surface back toward the viewer. In real-time rendering, reflections are approximated using techniques like cube maps, screen-space reflections, and planar reflection textures. Ray-traced reflections produce accurate results by tracing actual ray paths, but at higher computational cost.

resources.title: How Can We Use Reflection in Game Development?

nodes.name: Diffuse
nodes.description: In the world of 3D rendering and game development, "diffuse" refers to diffuse lighting or diffuse reflection. It's a key concept in making objects look three-dimensional and realistically lit.

resources.title: Difference Between Albedo and Diffuse Map
Complete Guide to Learn Texture Styles

nodes.name: Computer Animation
nodes.description: Computer animation covers techniques for producing motion in 3D scenes, including skeletal animation, blend shapes, procedural animation, and physics-based simulation. In games, animation systems must run in real time and blend smoothly between different motion clips based on gameplay state. Tools like animation state machines, inverse kinematics, and motion capture pipelines are all part of this area.

nodes.name: Color
nodes.description: Color in computer graphics is represented using color models such as RGB, HSV, and CIELAB, each suited to different tasks. Understanding color spaces, gamma correction, and the difference between linear and perceptual workflows is important for producing consistent results across displays and rendering pipelines. Physically based rendering typically works in linear light space and converts to a display color space at the end of the pipeline.

nodes.name: Ray Tracing
nodes.description: Ray tracing is a rendering technique that simulates light by tracing paths from the camera through each pixel into the scene, calculating intersections with geometry and recursively following reflected, refracted, and shadow rays. It produces physically accurate shadows, reflections, and global illumination but is computationally expensive. Hardware-accelerated ray tracing is now available through APIs like DirectX Raytracing and Vulkan Ray Tracing.

nodes.name: Visual Perception
nodes.description: Visual perception in graphics refers to how the human visual system interprets rendered images, including sensitivity to contrast, color, motion, and depth. Rendering techniques are often designed to exploit or match perceptual characteristics rather than achieve physical accuracy. Concepts like just-noticeable differences, chromatic adaptation, and saccadic masking influence decisions in both real-time and offline rendering.

nodes.name: Rasterization
nodes.description: Rasterization is the standard rendering technique used in real-time graphics, where 3D geometry is projected onto a 2D screen and filled with pixel colors based on shading calculations. It is much faster than ray tracing but requires additional techniques like shadow mapping, screen-space reflections, and ambient occlusion to approximate lighting effects that ray tracing handles natively.

nodes.name: Lighting and Shadow
nodes.description: Lighting and shadow systems determine how light sources illuminate a scene and how objects block that light to cast shadows. Real-time engines use a combination of dynamic lights, shadow maps, and baked light data to balance visual quality and performance. Shadow techniques include shadow mapping, stencil shadows, and ray-traced shadows.

nodes.name: Tone Reproduction
nodes.description: Tone reproduction, also called tone mapping, is the process of converting high dynamic range (HDR) scene luminance values into the limited range that a display can show. Since real-world lighting varies across many orders of magnitude, tone mapping operators compress this range while preserving perceived contrast and detail. Common operators include Reinhard, ACES filmic, and Uncharted 2.

nodes.name: Graphics Pipeline
nodes.description: The graphics pipeline is the sequence of stages that transforms 3D geometry into a final 2D image on screen. It includes stages like vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shading, and output merging. Modern pipelines expose programmable stages through vertex and fragment shaders, with newer APIs supporting additional stages like mesh shaders and ray tracing pipelines.

nodes.name: Shadow Map
nodes.description: A shadow map is a depth texture rendered from the light's point of view, used to determine which parts of the scene are in shadow when rendering from the camera. Each fragment is compared to the stored depth value; if it is farther from the light than what the shadow map records, it is shadowed. Shadow maps are the most common real-time shadowing technique and come in several variants including cascaded shadow maps and cube shadow maps for point lights.

resources.title: A Beginner's Guide to Shadow Mapping

nodes.name: Light Source
nodes.description: A light source in 3D rendering is an entity that emits light and contributes to the illumination of the scene. Different light types produce different shading and shadow characteristics and must be configured according to the lighting design of the scene.

nodes.name: Sampling
nodes.description: Sampling in graphics refers to how discrete values are taken from continuous signals such as textures or light distributions. Aliasing artifacts appear when a scene contains detail at frequencies higher than the sampling rate, which is why techniques like multisampling, supersampling, and temporal anti-aliasing are used. Importance sampling is also central to Monte Carlo rendering methods.

nodes.name: 2D
nodes.description: 2D Game Development involves creating games in a two-dimensional plane, utilizing flat graphics and typically making use of x and y coordinates. From classic arcade games of the ’80s and ’90s to the rich array of indie games today, 2D game development is a vibrant and diverse sector of the gaming industry. Not only are 2D games visually appealing and nostalgic, but they’re also often more accessible for developers to create due to the simpler mechanics compared to 3D game development.

nodes.name: Cube
nodes.description: In computer graphics, "cube" in the context of shadows often refers to using a cube-shaped object to visualize the concept of a "shadow volume." Imagine a light source shining on a cube. The silhouette of the cube from the light's perspective, extended infinitely outwards, forms a volume. Any object inside this "shadow volume" is considered to be in shadow. While helpful for understanding, shadow volumes themselves are not always shaped like cubes - their complexity depends on the object casting the shadow.

nodes.name: Directional
nodes.description: Directional light simulates a distant light source like the sun. It has only a direction, not a specific position, meaning its light rays are parallel and cast consistent shadows regardless of object location within the scene. This makes it ideal for simulating sunlight or moonlight, providing realistic outdoor lighting while being relatively performant for rendering.

nodes.name: Spot
nodes.description: Spotlights are a common type of light in computer graphics and games that mimic the behavior of real-world spotlights. They offer a range of parameters to adjust their behavior, such as radius, cone angle, falloff, and intensity Spotlights are readily available out of the box in both Unreal and Unity game engines, making them an accessible and powerful tool for adding realistic and dynamic lighting to your scenes.

nodes.name: Shader
nodes.description: Shaders are a type of software used in 3D computer graphics. They are utilized to render quality visual effects by making calculations and transformations on image data. Also, a shader is responsible for determining the final color of an object. There are several types of shaders: vertex shaders, geometry shaders, pixel shaders, and compute shaders. Each of these is programmed to manipulate specific attributes of an image, such as its vertices, pixels, and overall geometry. They are essential tools for game developers aiming to produce realistic and engaging visual experiences.

resources.title: What Are Shaders in Video Games?
A Beginner's Guide to Coding Graphics Shaders

nodes.name: HLSL
nodes.description: HLSL (High-Level Shader Language) is the shader programming language used with DirectX. It compiles to GPU bytecode and supports all shader stages including vertex, pixel, compute, and ray tracing shaders. HLSL syntax resembles C and is the standard for shaders targeting Direct3D pipelines.

nodes.name: GLSL
nodes.description: GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language) is the shader language for OpenGL and Vulkan (via SPIR-V compilation). It follows a C-like syntax and supports vertex, fragment, geometry, tessellation, and compute shader stages. GLSL shaders are compiled at runtime by the driver in OpenGL or compiled to SPIR-V ahead of time for Vulkan.

nodes.name: Graphics API
nodes.description: A graphics API is a software interface that allows applications to communicate with the GPU to submit rendering commands, manage resources, and control the rendering pipeline. Modern low-level APIs like Vulkan, DirectX 12, and Metal give developers more explicit control over GPU resources and synchronization compared to older APIs. Choosing an API determines which platforms the renderer can target and how much driver overhead is involved.

nodes.name: Cascaded
nodes.description: Cascaded usually refers to cascaded shadow maps, a technique for rendering realistic shadows over a large area.

nodes.name: Infinite
nodes.description: Infinite refers to concept that deals with rendering scenes or objects that extend beyond the visible boundaries of the screen. This is crucial for creating immersive environments, as it allows developers to simulate vast landscapes or endless spaces without the need to render every detail at once. Techniques such as level of detail (LOD), culling, and procedural generation are often employed to manage performance while maintaining the illusion of infinity.

nodes.name: Point
nodes.description: Point lights are one of the most common types of lights used in computer graphics and games. They resemble real-world light bulbs, emitting light uniformly in all directions. These lights are available out of the box in most game engines and offer a range of customizable parameters, such as intensity, falloff, color, and more. Point lights are the most straightforward type of light, making them ideal for quickly and intuitively lighting up your scenes.

nodes.name: SPIR-V
nodes.description: `SPIR-V` is a binary intermediate language for graphics and computation kernels, which is defined by the Khronos Group. This programming language has been largely adopted and used by Vulkan, a low-overhead, cross-platform 3D graphics and computing API. Vulkan consumes `SPIR-V` directly, serving as the final shader stage before the GPU. The `SPIR-V` binary format is designed for portability and flexibility, allowing it to be a powerful tool for developers because of its extensibility through the addition of new instructions, without the need to rebuild toolchains or shaders. This makes `SPIR-V` an essential part of Vulkan, especially for game developers creating large, diverse worldscapes and intricate graphics.

resources.title: SPIR Overview - The Khronos Group Inc
SPIR-V - OpenGL Wiki - The Khronos Group

nodes.name: Visibility and Occlusion
nodes.description: Visibility and occlusion systems determine which parts of a scene are visible from the camera and which are hidden behind other geometry. These systems are used to skip rendering work for geometry that cannot be seen, improving performance. Techniques include frustum culling, occlusion culling, and portal-based visibility.

nodes.name: DirectX
nodes.description: **DirectX** is a collection of Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) developed by Microsoft to handle tasks related to multimedia, especially game programming and video, on Microsoft platforms. It was first introduced in 1995 and has become a crucial component for PC gaming. DirectX serves as an intermediary between a hardware and a software, managing the state of the hardware and giving commands to it. Some technologies under DirectX includes Direct3D for 3D graphics, DirectDraw for 2D graphics, DirectSound for sound, and DirectInput for interfacing with input devices such as keyboard and mouse.

nodes.name: OpenGL
nodes.description: OpenGL is a cross-platform graphics API that provides a high-level interface for 2D and 3D rendering. It has been widely used in games and applications since the 1990s but has largely been superseded by Vulkan for high-performance use cases. OpenGL remains common in tools, educational contexts, and platforms where Vulkan support is unavailable.

nodes.name: Vulkan
nodes.description: Vulkan is a low-level, cross-platform graphics API developed by the Khronos Group. It offers explicit control over GPU memory, synchronization, and command submission, reducing driver overhead compared to OpenGL. Vulkan is used for high-performance rendering on Windows, Linux, and Android and serves as the foundation for MoltenVK on Apple platforms.

nodes.name: Occluder
nodes.description: An occluder is a piece of geometry that blocks the view of objects behind it. In occlusion culling systems, occluders are used to test whether other objects are hidden and can therefore be skipped during rendering. Occluders are often simplified versions of scene geometry to keep the occlusion queries fast.

resources.title: Occluder and How to Use Them

nodes.name: Culling
nodes.description: **Culling** is a performance optimization strategy employed in game development to improve efficiency and speed. Culling helps in reducing the rendering workload by eliminating the elements that are not visible to the player or are outside the viewport of the game. There are several types of culling, two main being; **frustum culling** and **occlusion culling**. Frustum culling involves eliminating objects that are outside of the camera's field of view. On the other hand, Occlusion culling discards objects that are hidden or blocked by other objects. Culling ensures that only the elements that are necessary or add value to the player's experience are processed.

nodes.name: Clipping
nodes.description: Culling is the process of eliminating geometry that does not need to be rendered, either because it is outside the view frustum, occluded by other objects, or facing away from the camera. Effective culling reduces the number of draw calls and the amount of geometry the GPU must process. Common forms include frustum culling, occlusion culling, and backface culling.

nodes.name: Fog
nodes.description: Fog in game development refers to a visual effect used to simulate atmospheric conditions and enhance the depth perception in a game environment. It creates a gradient of visibility, often fading objects into the background, which can improve performance by reducing the number of objects rendered at a distance. Fog can be implemented in various ways, such as linear fog, which gradually obscures objects based on their distance from the camera, or exponential fog, which creates a more dramatic effect by rapidly increasing the density of fog with distance.

nodes.name: Specular
nodes.description: `Specular` reflections are mirror-like reflections. In these cases, the rays of light are reflected, more than they are absorbed. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, that is to say that the angle at which the light enters the medium and then bounces off, the angle of the beam that bounced off would be the same.

resources.title: Specular Reflection - Regular Reflection, Mirrors, Diffuse Reflection

nodes.name: Bump
nodes.description: Bump mapping is a technique that perturbs surface normals at the pixel level to create the illusion of small-scale surface detail without adding geometry. The original method stored height values in a grayscale texture and derived normals from it. Normal mapping replaced it in most applications by storing the perturbed normals directly.

resources.title: Normals, Normal maps and Bump maps

nodes.name: OpenGL ES
nodes.description: OpenGL ES (Open Graphics Library for Embedded Systems) is a subset of the OpenGL specification designed specifically for mobile and embedded devices, such as smartphones, tablets, and consoles. It provides a cross-platform API that allows developers to communicate directly with the device's Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) to render 2D and 3D computer graphics. By offering a streamlined set of commands for hardware acceleration, it enables high-performance rendering while managing the memory and power constraints typical of portable hardware.

resources.title: LVGL — Light and Versatile Embedded Graphics Library

nodes.name: Parallax
nodes.description: Parallax mapping is an enhancement over bump and normal mapping that offsets UV coordinates based on a height map and the viewing angle, giving surfaces a greater sense of depth. At steep angles, basic parallax mapping breaks down, so variants like parallax occlusion mapping add iterative ray stepping to improve accuracy for surfaces with significant height variation.

nodes.name: Metal
nodes.description: Metal is Apple's low-level graphics and compute API for iOS, macOS, iPadOS, and tvOS. It provides direct access to the GPU with minimal driver overhead and integrates tightly with Apple's hardware and development tools. Metal is the required graphics API for high-performance rendering on Apple devices.

nodes.name: Horizon
nodes.description: In graphics, the horizon refers to a horizontal line that represents the visual boundary where the sky meets the earth or a flat surface, such as the ocean. It's a fundamental concept in perspective and art, serving as a reference point for creating a sense of depth and distance in an image. The placement of the horizon line can significantly impact the composition and mood of an image, with high or low horizon lines creating different effects on the viewer's perception of the scene.

nodes.name: Game AI
nodes.description: Game AI is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) that is used to create video game characters that act and react like real human players. Game AI is used in a variety of video games, from simple puzzle games to complex strategy games. Game AI can be used to create non-player characters (NPCs) that interact with the player, as well as to create intelligent opponents that challenge the player.

nodes.name: Frustum
nodes.description: Frustum culling is a standard practice in computer graphics, used in virtually all games to optimize performance by not rendering objects outside of your field of view. Think of your field of view as a frustum, a truncated pyramid shape. The farthest side is called the far clip plane, and the closest side is the near clip plane. Any object in the game that doesn't fall within this frustum is culled, meaning it’s not rendered, to improve performance. This feature comes built-in with Unreal Engine.

resources.title: Frustum Culling - Game Optimization 101 - Unreal Engine

nodes.name: Polygon
nodes.description: In computer graphics and game development, a polygon is a 2D or 3D shape composed of a set of vertices connected by edges. Polygons are used to represent objects, characters, and environments in games and simulations.

nodes.name: Light
nodes.description: Light refers to a visual representation of illumination in a 3D environment. It is used to simulate the way light behaves in the real world, adding depth, volume, and realism to objects and scenes. Lighting can be categorized into different types, such as ambient, diffuse, specular, and emissive, each serving a specific purpose in creating a believable and immersive visual experience. Proper lighting can greatly enhance the mood, atmosphere, and overall aesthetic of a scene, making it an essential aspect of graphics and game development.

nodes.name: Polyhedron
nodes.description: In computer graphics and game development, a polyhedron is a 3D shape composed of a set of polygons that enclose a volume. Polyhedra are used to represent objects, characters, and environments in games and simulations.

nodes.name: Shadow
nodes.description: Shadows play a crucial role in enhancing the realism and depth of scenes in video games. They help to create a more immersive experience by simulating how light interacts with objects in a 3D environment.

resources.title: Real Time Shadow Casting using Shadow Volumes

nodes.name: WebGL
nodes.description: WebGL is a JavaScript API for rendering 2D and 3D graphics in a browser using the GPU, based on OpenGL ES 2.0 and 3.0. It runs without plugins and is supported in all major browsers. WebGL is used for browser-based games, data visualizations, and interactive 3D experiences.

nodes.name: Decision Making
nodes.description: Decision making in game AI governs how an NPC chooses what action to take based on its current state and environment. The goal is to produce behavior that appears intelligent and responsive to the player without being predictable or computationally expensive. Architectures like behavior trees, state machines, and utility systems are the primary tools.

nodes.name: Movement
nodes.description: Movement in game AI covers how characters navigate and move through the game world. This includes steering behaviors for local movement, pathfinding for navigating around obstacles, and crowd simulation for managing groups of agents. Good movement AI makes characters feel responsive and spatially aware.

nodes.name: Naive Bayes Classifier
nodes.description: A Naive Bayes classifier is a probabilistic model that predicts class membership based on Bayes' theorem with the assumption that features are conditionally independent. In games, it can be used for tasks like recognizing player behavior patterns or classifying game states. It is fast to train and evaluate, making it practical for real-time use.

resources.title: Text Classification With Naive Bayes Classifier

nodes.name: Decision Tree
nodes.description: A decision tree is a hierarchical structure where each node tests a condition and branches to different subtrees based on the result. In game AI, decision trees are used to encode rules that determine NPC behavior, such as whether to attack, flee, or patrol. They are simple to understand and debug but can become large and difficult to maintain for complex behaviors.

nodes.name: Decision Learning
nodes.description: Decision learning refers to machine learning approaches that train models to make sequential choices, often in the form of learned decision trees or policy networks. In game contexts, it can be used to build NPCs that adapt their decision-making based on observed outcomes. It bridges classical rule-based systems and modern reinforcement learning.

nodes.name: Game AI
nodes.description: Game AI is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) that is used to create video game characters that act and react like real human players. Game AI is used in a variety of video games, from simple puzzle games to complex strategy games. Game AI can be used to create non-player characters (NPCs) that interact with the player, as well as to create intelligent opponents that challenge the player.

nodes.name: Learning
nodes.description: Machine Learning is a field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. It is a branch of artificial intelligence based on the idea that systems can learn from data, identify patterns and make decisions with minimal human intervention. In terms of game development, machine learning can be used to create NPCs that can learn from the player's actions and adapt to them.

nodes.name: Board Game
nodes.description: Board game AI refers to techniques for building agents that play turn-based strategy games like chess, checkers, Go, and similar abstractions. These games have well-defined rules and discrete state spaces, making them natural benchmarks for AI algorithms. Tree search methods like minimax and Monte Carlo Tree Search dominate this area.

nodes.name: State Machine
nodes.description: A finite state machine (FSM) is a model where an entity can exist in one of a finite set of states and transitions between states based on defined conditions. In game AI, FSMs control character behavior by mapping states like idle, patrol, and attack to specific actions and defining the triggers that switch between them. They are easy to implement but can become unwieldy with many states and transitions.

nodes.name: Reinforcements Learning
nodes.description: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent to maximize a cumulative reward signal by taking actions in an environment and observing the results. In games, RL has been used to train superhuman game-playing agents and is increasingly used for NPC behavior, playtesting, and animation control. Common algorithms include Q-learning, PPO, and SAC.

resources.title: AI Learns to Walk (Deep Reinforcement Learning)

nodes.name: Minimax
nodes.description: `Minimax` is an artificial intelligence (AI) decision-making algorithm mainly used in decision making and game theory, particularly for two player zero-sum games. It formulates a strategy by simulating all possible game scenarios and assuming that the opponent is playing an optimal game. Minimax operates by the player minimizing the possible loss for a worst case scenario and thus making the 'maximum of the minimum' possible scenarios. This algorithm is often combined with `alpha-beta pruning` technique to increase its efficiency.

nodes.name: Behavior Tree
nodes.description: A behavior tree is a hierarchical control structure used to define complex NPC behaviors through composable nodes. Internal nodes like sequences, selectors, and decorators control the flow of execution, while leaf nodes represent individual actions or conditions. Behavior trees are more modular and easier to extend than large state machines and are widely used in commercial game AI.

resources.title: Unreal Engine 5 Tutorial - AI Part 2: Behavior Tree

nodes.name: Decision Tree Learning
nodes.description: Decision tree learning is a supervised machine learning method that builds a tree model from labeled training data by recursively splitting the data on the most informative features. In game AI, it can be used to learn behavior rules from recorded gameplay or designer-specified examples. Algorithms like ID3 and CART are standard approaches.

resources.title: Game Strategy - Real Time Decision Tree

nodes.name: AB Pruning
nodes.description: Alpha-beta pruning is an optimization of the minimax algorithm that eliminates branches of the game tree that cannot influence the final decision. It maintains two values, alpha and beta, representing the minimum score the maximizing player is assured and the maximum score the minimizing player is assured. When a node's score falls outside this window, its subtree is pruned, significantly reducing the search space without affecting the result.

resources.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning: A Deep Dive into its History

nodes.name: Fuzzy Logic
nodes.description: Fuzzy logic allows AI systems to work with degrees of truth rather than binary true/false values. In games, it is used to make NPC decision-making more gradual and natural, for example allowing a character to be "somewhat aggressive" rather than simply aggressive or not. Fuzzy systems define membership functions for each state variable and apply fuzzy rules to derive outputs.

nodes.name: Deep Learning
nodes.description: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical representations of data. In game development, deep learning is applied to tasks like AI game agents, procedural content generation, animation synthesis, and image upscaling. Its ability to handle raw sensory input like pixels makes it particularly useful for agents that interact with games directly through visual observations.

nodes.name: MCTS
nodes.description: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a search algorithm that builds a game tree by randomly simulating game play-outs and using the results to guide further exploration. It balances exploration of unknown branches with exploitation of known good moves using the UCB1 formula. MCTS is well-suited to games with large branching factors and is the backbone of AlphaGo and similar systems.

nodes.name: Markov System
nodes.description: A Markov system in game AI models behavior as a set of states with probabilistic transitions between them. At each step, the system transitions to the next state based on probability weights, producing varied and non-deterministic NPC behavior. Markov chains can generate natural-looking animation transitions, dialogue, and patrol patterns.

resources.title: Using Markov Chain in Game Development

nodes.name: Artificial Neural Network
nodes.description: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model loosely inspired by biological neurons, consisting of layers of interconnected units that process input signals and produce outputs. Neural networks are trained by adjusting weights through backpropagation to minimize prediction error. In games, ANNs are used as policy functions in RL agents, behavior classifiers, and procedural generation systems.

nodes.name: Advanced Rendering
nodes.description: Advanced rendering covers techniques that go beyond standard rasterization to produce more realistic or visually sophisticated output. This includes physically based rendering, global illumination, ray tracing, and post-processing effects. These techniques require deeper understanding of light physics and more complex GPU programming.

nodes.name: Goal Oriented Behavior
nodes.description: Goal oriented behavior in game development refers to the artificial intelligence algorithms employed that give non-player characters (NPCs) the ability to make decisions based on certain objectives or tasks. These NPCs analyze the circumstances in the game environment, formulate a plan to achieve specific goals, and then execute it. The degree of sophistication in these algorithms can range from simple pathways to complex problem-solving solutions. As the behavior models are not hard-coded, it provides NPCs with greater adaptability and autonomy.

nodes.name: Physically-Based Rendering
nodes.description: Physically-based rendering (PBR) is a shading approach that models the interaction of light with surfaces based on physical principles such as energy conservation and the Fresnel effect. It uses standardized material parameters like base color, roughness, and metalness, which produce consistent results under different lighting conditions. PBR has become the standard shading model in modern real-time and offline rendering pipelines.

nodes.name: Microsurface Scattering
nodes.description: Microsurface scattering describes how light interacts with the microscopic irregularities of a surface, which are too small to model with geometry but affect the overall reflectance. PBR materials use microfacet models like GGX or Beckmann to represent the statistical distribution of these tiny surface normals. The roughness parameter controls how broad or sharp the resulting specular highlight appears.

nodes.name: Real-time Ray Tracing
nodes.description: Real-time ray tracing uses dedicated hardware acceleration, such as NVIDIA RTX or AMD RDNA ray tracing cores, to trace rays into the scene at interactive frame rates. It enables effects like accurate reflections, shadows, and ambient occlusion that are difficult to fake convincingly with rasterization. Real-time ray tracing is typically used selectively, combining traced rays with rasterized output to balance quality and performance.

nodes.name: DirectX Ray Tracing
nodes.description: DirectX Raytracing (DXR) is Microsoft's extension to Direct3D 12 that exposes hardware ray tracing capabilities through a set of new pipeline stages and shader types including ray generation, intersection, any-hit, closest-hit, and miss shaders. DXR integrates ray tracing into the existing D3D12 rendering pipeline and is available on Windows 10 and later. It is the primary ray tracing API for Windows-based game development.

nodes.name: Translucency & Transparency
nodes.description: Translucency and transparency describe different ways light passes through a material. Transparent materials allow light to pass through without scattering, like glass, while translucent materials scatter light as it passes through, like skin or wax. Rendering these effects in real time requires techniques like alpha blending, order-independent transparency, and subsurface scattering approximations.

nodes.name: Vulkan Ray Tracing
nodes.description: Vulkan Ray Tracing is the Khronos Group's extension to Vulkan that exposes hardware-accelerated ray tracing across platforms. It uses the same shader stage model as DXR and supports acceleration structure management for efficient scene traversal. Vulkan Ray Tracing provides cross-platform ray tracing support on Windows, Linux, and Android.

nodes.name: Conservation of Energy
nodes.description: Conservation of energy in rendering means that a surface cannot reflect more light than it receives. PBR shading models enforce this principle by ensuring that the sum of diffuse and specular contributions does not exceed the incoming irradiance. Violating energy conservation produces unnaturally bright surfaces that break physical plausibility.

nodes.name: OptiX
nodes.description: OptiX is NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated ray tracing API and SDK, designed for high-performance offline and real-time ray tracing on CUDA-capable hardware. It provides a programmable pipeline for ray tracing with support for custom intersection, shading, and miss programs. OptiX is widely used in offline rendering, scientific visualization, and research rather than mainstream game development.

nodes.name: Metallicity
nodes.description: Metallicity, also called metalness, is a PBR material parameter that describes whether a surface behaves like a metal or a dielectric. Metals have no diffuse component and highly colored specular reflections, while dielectrics have diffuse color and white specular highlights. The metalness parameter in PBR workflows blends between these two behaviors.
